preamble: Merger of Classical Arabic ḍād ض, reconstructed as [ɮˤ], with ẓāʾ ظ [ðˤ]: the lateral fricative becomes central. In most Arabic vernaculars the two letters 'merged quite early' (Versteegh 1999, cited by Wikipedia), and in varieties that keep the dental fricatives, such as Najdi, Tunisian and Mesopotamian Arabic, both are [ðˤ] (Wikipedia, Ḍād; Al Motairi 2015: 7 for Najdi, cited by Wikipedia). In Gulf Arabic the merged reflex is a fricative, [ðˤ] or [zˤ] (Holes 2001: 51; Khalifa et al. 2016, cited by Wikipedia), and ض and ظ are not distinguished in pronunciation (Qafisheh 1977: 2, cited by Wikipedia). In Hassaniya, /ð̣/ is 'the normal equivalent' of Classical ض, while /ḍ/ appears in loans from Standard Arabic, so pairs such as staḥḍaṛ 'to be in agony' and staḥð̣aṛ 'to remember' separate a learned from a dialectal meaning (Taine-Cheikh 2020: 248). Not every variety merged: Tihāmah dialects keep a lateral, with [ɬˤ ~ ɮˤ] and [ðˤ] as allophones for both letters (Alqahtani 2015: 45–46, cited by Wikipedia), and some keep distinct reflexes of ḍ and ẓ (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 428). Where dental fricatives became stops, as in Egypt and the Levant, the merged sound went on to [dˤ]. The starting value [ɮˤ] is reconstructed from Sibawayh's description (Wikipedia, Ḍād).
